title: Workism, AI and Vocations
description:
Photo by Look Studio on Unsplash

Introduction

There is this truly great read in Noema: Why Is Everyone In Tech So Sad? by Aaron Horwath. One of the major points of this article is that Workism was used to replace religion in people’s lives. The idea that people looked for purpose in their work the way some people are called to vocations. And now, there seems to be a collapse in Workism that is leading to widespread disenchantment among knowledge workers.

One sentence in particular caught my attention:

That’s the true beauty of Workism: It is manufactured to distract people from the hole in their souls that a vocation would otherwise fill.

While that is the state of employment now, it wasn’t always the case. However, even in my case the end result is very similar.

My Time In Tech

I spent approximately thirty years in technology in multiple roles. I started off in development, moved into documentation, technical support, and finally into infrastructure. The ladder I climbed literally doesn’t exist today.

It wasn’t my plan to leave the tech industry when I did. Due to personal reasons I had to relocate to take care of family. When I looked at the job market in this area it became clear pretty quickly: this wasn’t the market for my skill set. This market wants the jack-of-all-trades (master-of-none). Whereas, while I wouldn’t call myself a master, I have a highly defined set of skills (and now I wouldn’t even consider it to have kept up).

This was ten years ago. I’m honestly glad I didn’t even try to go back into tech.

The Underlying Tension

Even before this situation arose I had felt tension in the IT field. And it wasn’t some specific change in the technology, the training, or knowledge. All of those things can be solved. No, this was a change in the relationship that I had with work. This was a change in how I defined myself, and how I was becoming more and more of a misfit in the field that I had spent so long in.

A lot of this centered on employer expectations. In my early employment there were things that were enjoyable about the jobs. There was interesting technology to experience. There were interesting problems to be solved. And, more than anything, there was a form of camaraderie with my coworkers. We shared this sense of adventure, and joy that the job brought us.

But over time that changed. Probably because early on we were on the cutting edge of so many things. Honestly, when I started, most IT people wouldn’t allow an x86 server in their server room. They were still dominated by HP, IBM and Sun. By the time I left, HP and IBM were exceptions, and Sun’s platforms were x86 based.

What happened during this time was likely predictable. Early on companies looked for people with knowledge and experience in this new hardware. The IBM PC and Louts 1-2-3 had been a curveball thrown at the IT departments of many of these companies. Companies responded by finding people that were knowledgeable about the technology, but not necessarily knowledgeable about IT.

And, also during this time, IT itself went under a transformation. In the days of mainframes and minicomputers IT was an expense. It was something that was paid for, and the bean counters didn’t really understand how to quantify IT. But around this time IT departments found themselves being changed from an expense based to cost based. In other words, the accountants had been given the directive to understand the value of IT, how to quantify it in dollars instead of it just being a black hole of expense.

My Perspective

As I moved from one employer to the next I found the requirements for the jobs changing. Things like NDA’s were being introduced. Uncompensated overtime in the form of “on-call” duty became a standard. Allocations for training were reduced. Budgets were always big enough to get the newest toy some business department wanted, and the IT people were told to deal with it instead of being consulted on the viability of these systems.1

When I started in the industry I worked for small companies. And there was a definite element of “Workism” in those companies. We put in long hours and lived for the jobs. But we were all enjoying, at least at some level, what we were doing. There were things we were getting to experience through our jobs that we never would have been able to anywhere else.

But, several jobs later, I started separating my identity from the workplace. The rigidity of the structures put in place between HR and Accounting sucked most of the fun out of being an employee. Instead, it was more like being a drone, a worker bee. The changes that were force on IT departments by clueless managers changed the dynamics of the work environment, and not for the better.

At first, I engaged with different technologies outside of work that I knew weren’t going to become part of my work environment. But then when most of that started running dry for me, I turned to other things.

Re-Finding My Vocation(s)

I wasn’t a computer science major in school. I had started down that road, but had found it to be less interesting to me. I had other interests, mostly leaning towards the arts. Music was a particular interest to me. But, then, in college I found myself wandering into the writing program, and ended up becoming an English major.

I never graduated from college. But that wasn’t an issue in the early days of x86 technology invading corporations. There were plenty of opportunities for anyone that could reasonably demonstrate that they had a needed skill set and were competent. I had basically found myself moving into the IT field because: (a) It offered stable employment. (b) My parents (my father in particular) didn’t like the idea of his son becoming an artist / musician / writer / etc. My father equated it with “being a bum."2

As employers tried to push their employees further in one direction, I started rediscovering the vocations I’d had before. I started finding issues that I was concerned about, and joined a podcast to talk about both technology and social aspects of technology.

Then I started found a whole new love and appreciation for music. The music industry had become this quagmire of manure, so I started getting into music that wasn’t from the major labels. All of this led to a series of projects that were about the person I was and still am: A blog where I reviewed indie music. A podcast where I played a lot of the music I had curated. And finally my own little indie music label.

But all of those were set aside when I left the tech industry. Not because I didn’t want to keep them going, but because I had personal responsibilities that I had to prioritize above them.

Hobbies Become Vocations

When the personal responsibilities I had left the tech industry to handle were concluded, I found myself with a lot of time on my hands. I found myself in a new place in my life, a place where I could pursue whatever I wanted to.

The first thing that came to my mind was to start into a loosely tech related hobby. Kind of a low-tech hobby. But my interest in that hobby waned, but it didn’t disappear. Then I started turning myself towards several other hobbies, the majority of which took me away from tech.

I’ve been writing about these hobbies on Ennui Vagaries.

But the biggest turn around happened when I realized that I wanted to get back to one of my big vocations: writing. Experimenting in writing with fountain pens led me to find the joy and purpose in my writing again. Eschewing the CMS platform that no longer fit for my writing process led me to find new platforms that are a much better fit.

And because of this newly re-found joy, I am back to writing posts daily. On three different blogs, each with a different focus. This is the life that I have wanted to have back, and I only found my way back to it by getting out of the tech space.

It’s a Cycle Repeating Again and Again

The article asks questions about what happens when the spell of “Workism” is popped:

What would happen, then, if something threatened that faith? A paradigm shift that broke the spell of Workism? A sort of enlightenment that caused Knowledge Workers to start asking tough questions of their organizations and themselves.

I would posit that this isn’t new. It’s a cycle that happens to every generation. We’ve seen it many times, albeit most of the time it’s not as loud as the current circumstances.

For example, in my early career many developers were used to writing code to the bare metal. DOS didn’t offer a lot of facilities. Developers used libraries to access low level functions of the system. Those were mostly I/O related. They weren’t some class system for accessing a window manager. Then came the web and java, and the whole paradigm shifted again. And there were a lot of developers that just left. It wasn’t fun for them if the low-level bare-metal coding went away.

There was a developer who was well known in the Open Source community who just shut everything down. He posted that he had left his job, and was leaving behind the projects that he had worked on for years. He was disabling his phone, and abandoning all communication in the online world.

My personal journey evolved around multiple factors, the biggest of them being the continual creeping enshittification of the work environment. Eventually I found that my skills, while highly desirable at the time, AFAIK, weren’t applicable in my current job market. And that’s when I realized it was time to let go.

The only difference I see now is this one is landing with a kerthunk, potentially hitting tens or hundreds of thousands of “knowledge workers” all at once. And my response is:

Welcome to the cycle.

Time to find your vocation and start rebuilding your life.

  2. I could, and likely will at some point, write more about my father’s perspective of employment. I have written a little about it before, but there is more to be said. ↩︎

title: The Handmade Surface: Imperfection, Texture, and Craft in Contemporary Chinese Interiors
description: Craft in contemporary interiors is increasingly valuable in the way materials are joined and brought into relation with one another. As the appetite for fast, inexpensive, and profitable retrofitting grows, there is also a parallel desire for interiors that feel thoughtfully resolved: spaces where details are integrated, material assemblies are considered, textures transition with intention, and hardware is treated as part of the architectural language rather than an afterthought. In many contemporary Chinese interiors, craft operates quietly through the treatment of surfaces and structures: timber that retains its irregularity, terrazzo that records aggregate and handwork, or finishes that reveal the care of their making.

title: Why Travel (still) Shapes the Way Architects Think
description: Between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, traveling through Rome, Paris, Venice, Florence, and other European cities was considered an essential part of a newly graduated architect's education. At a time when access to photographs and publications was extremely limited, these trips were the primary way to experience architecture up close. In the early twentieth century, Le Corbusier reinterpreted this tradition in his own way: at 23, he embarked on the Voyage d'Orient, passing through the Balkans, Istanbul, and Athens, producing travel notebooks he would return to throughout his life.

title: Hungary's New Architectural Landscape: Building From the Past
description: Hungary's architectural landscape spent the socialist decades being redrawn from above, its cooperative farms consolidated out of family plots and its standardized housing blocks distributed across the territory in a form that would have been identical anywhere else. The sociologist Virág Molnár, whose Building the State traces the political uses of architecture in postwar Hungary and East Germany, has made the case that this reshaping of the built environment was one of the political project's primary instruments and not a byproduct of it, a mobilization that carried through socialist modernization and into the transition that followed. The British critic Owen Hatherley, whose Landscapes of Communism explores the housing estates of Budapest alongside those of Warsaw and Kyiv, describes the far end of that same inheritance, where buildings have outlasted the ideology that commissioned them and remain occupied by people with little stake in defending the reasoning behind them.

title: Healthcare has enough front doors—it needs fewer dead ends
description:
Healthcare has spent the last decade building front doors.

There are digital front doors for health systems, telehealth platforms for urgent needs, benefit portals for covered services, online price transparency tools, pharmacy apps, manufacturer savings programs, navigation companies, and condition-specific care models. Each one promises to help people find a way into our highly complex healthcare system.

That progress matters. More entry points can make care easier to discover, compare, and initiate. But for many consumers, the hardest part of healthcare is navigating their way to what comes next.

HEALTHCARE BREAKS DOWN IN THE HANDOFFS

A consumer may start with a telehealth visit, then need a prescription, then realize the medication is not covered or costs more than expected. Another may find a lower price online, then struggle to understand whether it is covered there by their insurance or at their preferred pharmacy. Someone else may be told to get a lab, scan, or follow-up visit, only to face yet another search for availability, pricing, and payment options.

The problem is that too many of these steps end in uncertainty.

That is where healthcare loses people. And the worst part is it usually occurs at a critical point in their treatment journey: when they’re deciding whether to seek care in the handoffs between diagnosis, cost, coverage, fulfillment, and follow-through. In those moments, intent becomes action or turns into delay.

ACCESS MUST INCLUDE FOLLOW-THROUGH

The healthcare industry has put significant energy into helping people start their care journey. The next challenge is putting equal effort into helping them continue.

In most consumer industries, a good experience is defined by whether the experience holds together after the first click. Travel platforms like Expedia or Google Flights do not just show that flights exist; they help consumers compare routes, understand prices, book, check in, and manage changes. And the same is true for retail apps: They show inventory and connect this seamlessly with payment, delivery, and returns.

EVERY DEAD END HAS A COST

Although healthcare is more complex and personal than these examples, that complexity makes follow-through more important.

When the experience breaks down, the consequences are serious. People delay appointments because they do not know what they will owe. Many abandon prescriptions when the price at the pharmacy counter is higher than expected. Some start treatment without a clear understanding of whether they can afford to continue, while others spend hours trying to connect pieces of the system that were never designed around the consumer experience.

These dead ends rarely happen in isolation. A coverage issue becomes a pricing issue. A pricing issue becomes a fulfillment issue. A fulfillment issue becomes an adherence issue. Sometimes the cost is financial. Other times it’s clinical. Almost always, it erodes trust in the system.

DESIGN FOR THE MOMENTS PEOPLE GET STUCK

Healthcare has given people more places to start. Now it’s time to make the path easier to navigate.

That requires designing around the moments when consumers are most likely to get stuck. When a prescription is written, people should be able to see relevant cost options before they reach the pharmacy counter. When a service is recommended, people should have a clearer understanding of what insurance may cover, the self-pay options, and what the next step will cost. When a treatment requires ongoing use, the experience should be built around continuity, not just initiation.

No single company can own every part of the journey. But every organization that touches that journey has a responsibility to reduce friction at the handoff. Providers, pharmacies, manufacturers, employers, payers, and technology platforms all shape whether someone can start and stay on therapy. But consumers should not be the only connective tissue among them. A better system would bring pricing, access, fulfillment, and support closer together so that fewer people are left to troubleshoot healthcare in real time.

FUTURE SUCCESS MODELS ARE ALREADY HERE

This is part of how we think about GoodRx Companion, our monthly subscription that brings together free and low-cost generic medications, affordable online care visits, and savings on routine services such as dental, vision, labs, and imaging. Companion is not meant to replace insurance. It is designed around the everyday healthcare needs that can become unnecessarily fragmented, giving consumers a more predictable place to manage routine costs and care.

The broader lesson is that healthcare experiences should be judged by accessibility in the enrollment process, and also by how well they help people move forward.

A digital tool that surfaces a price but does not help someone use it is only part of the answer. Same goes for a care model that starts with a visit but leaves cost and fulfillment unresolved or incomplete; or a benefit that technically exists but is too hard to understand or access.

Medical innovation will only make this more urgent. Breakthrough therapies can change lives, but their impact depends on whether people can access them, afford them, and stay on treatment. The same is true for routine care. Healthcare value is created when people can complete the path to care.

That is the design challenge for healthcare now: fewer disconnected experiences, fewer unclear next steps, and fewer moments when consumers have to stop and decode the system before they can keep going.

Healthcare has opened more doors than ever. Now it has to make sure those doors actually lead somewhere.

Wendy Barnes is president and CEO of GoodRx.

title: Frame 122 / Brent Buck Architects
description:
Frame 122 is a five-story, 30,725-square-foot mass-timber multifamily residential building that transforms a former parking garage into a sustainable, family-oriented community in Brooklyn's Clinton Hill neighborhood. Constructed with prefabricated cross-laminated timber (CLT) floor and roof panels, it is New York City's first mass-timber building approved under the 2022 Building Code.
The building contains fifteen two- and three-bedroom apartments organized around a shared open-air courtyard and connected by exterior walkways and stairs. Every residence has at least three solar exposures, providing abundant daylight, natural ventilation, and a strong connection to the outdoors. Shared circulation and outdoor spaces create opportunities for daily interaction while maintaining privacy within each home.

title: The real cost of engineering: churn and coupling
description:
What matters most in a company is where the focus is. In engineering, it is very easy to spend hours building solutions to problems that don’t exist, and then spend the following years maintaining them, fixing them, and untangling the coupling layers they’ve grown with other components.
Every company wastes resources this way. But companies without clear objectives, and without the courage to say “no”, will waste the majority of their resources this way, without ever noticing.

title: Beyond the Handmade Aesthetic: Why Craft Needs New Construction Economies
description: There has never been a more celebrated moment for craftsmanship in architecture. Across magazines, awards, and international exhibitions, handmade brick, lime plaster, carved stone, woven bamboo, and rammed earth have re-emerged as symbols of environmental responsibility, cultural continuity, and architectural authenticity. Beyond these carefully documented projects lies another reality. The overwhelming majority of buildings constructed today, from apartment blocks and office towers to public housing and commercial developments, continue to rely on industrialized systems that leave little room for skilled artisans. Craft has become increasingly visible at the very moment it has become increasingly uncommon. In countries such as India, the contrast is difficult to ignore. Centuries-old building traditions continue alongside one of the world's fastest-growing construction industries. To reframe the question of why craftsmanship is returning, perhaps the intrigue is why it now appears primarily where construction budgets, timelines, and clients can afford it.
